Note that [MATH: \mathbf T] and [MATH: \mathbf N] denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

sections.normalized_html:
To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector [MATH: \mathbf p] and a vector [MATH: \mathbf n] that is perpendicular to the osculating plane.

The position vector of the point where [MATH: t=0] is [MATH: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}(0) = \cos{0}\,\mathbf i+\cos{0}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{2}\sin{0}\, \mathbf k = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle.]

To compute the perpendicular vector, we first need to compute the unit tangent [MATH: \mathbf T(0)] and the principal normal [MATH: \mathbf N(0)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: T(0)|= (sqrt(2))/(2)(− \sin 0i − \sin 0j + sqrt(2)\cos 0k) = k; N(0)|= − (sqrt(2))/(2)(\cos 0i + \cos 0j + sqrt(2)\sin 0k) = − (sqrt(2))/(2)(i + j)]

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

[MATH: n|= k × (− (sqrt(2))/(2)(i + j)); = − (sqrt(2))/(2) ⋅ i|j|k; 0|0|1; 1|1|0; = − (sqrt(2))/(2)[0|1; 1|0i − 0|1; 1|0j + 0|0; 1|1k]; = − (sqrt(2))/(2)(− i + j); = (sqrt(2))/(2)(i − j)]

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction: [MATH: \mathbf{n} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 2}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(\mathbf i-\mathbf j\right) =\mathbf i-\mathbf j]

Finally, let [MATH: \langle x,y,z \rangle] denote the position vector of a general point in the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to [MATH: \mathbf{n}] and passes through the tip of the position vector [MATH: \mathbf{p},] its Cartesian equation can be written as

[MATH: (⟨x, y, z⟩ − p) ⋅ n|= 0; ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ n − p ⋅ n|= 0; ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ n|= p ⋅ n; ⟨x, y, z⟩ ⋅ ⟨1, − 1, 0⟩|= ⟨1, 1, 0⟩ ⋅ ⟨1, − 1, 0⟩; 1 ⋅ x + (− 1) ⋅ y + 0 ⋅ z|= 0; x − y|= 0.]

Note: Because our curve is a plane curve, it has the same osculating plane at each point. As shown above, the osculating plane coincides with the plane of the curve.

This result holds in general: any plane curve has the same osculating plane at each of its points (wherever the osculating plane is defined).

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the curve [MATH: C] parametrized by the vector function
[MATH: \mathbf f (t)= \big\langle2 \sin t, \: 2\cos t, \: t \big\rangle.]
At the point [MATH: P] where [MATH: t=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},] the function, unit tangent, and the principal normal are given by

Content:
[MATH: f((5π)/(6))|= (1)/(6)⟨6, − 6sqrt(3), 5π⟩; T((5π)/(6))|= (1)/(5)⟨ − sqrt(15), − sqrt(5), sqrt(5)⟩; N((5π)/(6))|= (1)/(2)⟨ − 1, sqrt(3), 0⟩.]

Content:
Since the unit tangent [MATH: \mathbf T] and the principal normal [MATH: \mathbf N] are not collinear, they define a unique plane, called the osculating plane. In general, the osculating plane to a curve at a point [MATH: P] is the plane of "greatest contact" with the curve at [MATH: P.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a6f5af0263486a52639abc1ba972c256]

Content:
Since the osculating plane contains the unit tangent vector and the principal normal vector, we can write the equation of the osculating plane in parametric form as follows:

Content:
[MATH: R(s, u)|= f((5π)/(6)) + sT((5π)/(6)) + uN((5π)/(6)); = (1)/(6)⟨6, − 6sqrt(3), 5π⟩ + (s)/(5)⟨ − sqrt(15), − sqrt(5), sqrt(5)⟩ + (u)/(2)⟨ − 1, sqrt(3), 0⟩]
where [MATH: s, u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
In general, for a curve [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t),] the osculating plane at the point [MATH: t=t_0] has the parametric equation
[MATH: \mathbf R(s,u) = \mathbf r \left( t_0 \right) + s \, \mathbf T \left( t_0 \right) + u \, \mathbf N \left( t_0 \right), \qquad s, u \in (-\infty, \infty),]
where [MATH: \mathbf{T}(t_0)] and [MATH: \mathbf{N}(t_0)] are the unit tangent and the principal normal to the curve at [MATH: t=t_0,] respectively.

Content:
Note: A straight line does not have a principal normal, and consequently it does not have an osculating plane either.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Parametric Equation of an Osculating Plane

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/4e137f91b31bc0f426210fdcf32b3801]

Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] at the point where [MATH: t=1,] given that

[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \left\langle -2t , \: t^2 , \: \dfrac{1}{3}t^3 \right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf T(1) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left\langle -2 , 2 , 1 \right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf N(1) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left\langle 2 , 1 , 2\right\rangle.]

Note that [MATH: \mathbf T] and [MATH: \mathbf N] denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The osculating plane passes through the point [MATH: P,] which is at the tip of the vector [MATH: \mathbf r(1).] The vectors [MATH: \mathbf T(1)] and [MATH: \mathbf N(1)] are parallel to this plane and are not collinear, so a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

[MATH: \mathbf R(s,u) = \mathbf r(1) + s \, \mathbf T(1) + u \, \mathbf N(1), \qquad s,u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf r(1),] we get

[MATH: r(1)|= ⟨ − 2(1), (1)^{2}, (1)/(3)(1)^{3}⟩ = ⟨ − 2, 1, (1)/(3)⟩.]

Therefore, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point [MATH: \left(-2,1,\dfrac 1 3 \right)] is given by

[MATH: R(s, u)|= r(1) + sT(1) + uN(1); = ⟨ − 2, 1, (1)/(3)⟩ + s ⋅ (1)/(3)⟨ − 2, 2, 1⟩ + u ⋅ (1)/(3)⟨2, 1, 2⟩; = (1)/(3)⟨ − 6 − 2s + 2u, 3 + 2s + u, 1 + s + 2u⟩.]
